transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-03
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Nora (Redwood Solutions), Jordan (CTO Helios), Priya (ML Infra), Ethan (SRE), Marta (Security), Sam (Data Scientist)

Summary: technical deep dive focused on autoscaling behavior for Redwood Dedicated and Private deployments. Topics: burst policies, queueing models, reserved GPU sizing, KV cache effects on latency, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, VPC/network constraints, and security/compliance touchpoints. Agreed to run a 1-week benchmark pilot and exchange security docs.

00:00:02 Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intro — i'm alex martinez, i'll run through the agenda. we're hoping to walk through autoscaling models, how reserved gpus + burst works, and then dig into your workloads.
00:00:18 Jordan (CTO): thanks, alex. we wanna understand cost/latency tradeoffs and how to size capacity for our peak loads — we do spiky traffic with nightly batch jobs and daytime API traffic.
00:00:30 Samir (SE): great. before we dive, can you share rough rps and token per request? that helps pick queueing models.
00:00:36 Priya (ML Infra): yeah — daytime peak is about 220 rps, median token length ~180 tokens, tail to 1k on big summarize jobs, and overnight batch runs up to 500 concurrent requests but they are async.
00:00:55 Alex (AE): perfect. couple quick notes: Redwood Dedicated supports reserved GPU pools with configurable burst capacity and queueing. You can set a steady baseline of reserved GPUs and allow burst to ephemeral nodes in the same region — this is controlled by burst_policy and queueing_strategy.
00:01:12 Priya: when you say ephemeral nodes — those are still in our VPC when using Private? i.e., on-prem or VPC Private?
00:01:20 Nora (Solutions Architect): good q. for Redwood Private (VPC), ephemeral instances are managed by the customer's infra or can be provisioned by Redwood agents depending on the deployment model. For hosted Dedicated they're in our infra but isolated to your pool. For VPC we integrate with your autoscaler (k8s/instance group).
00:01:40 Ethan (SRE): we care about cold start times. what are typical time-to-warm for a new GPU instance with your runtime and model?
00:01:48 Samir (SE): cold starts depend on model size & quantization. For a 13B quantized model it can be ~25-45s to load weights and initialize kernels; for a 70B it can be 60-120s. We mitigate that with a warm pool and pre-warming strategies and also checkpointed kv-cache warmup for active sessions.
00:02:10 Jordan: ok so we need to size a warm baseline to avoid cold starts impacting P95. how do you recommend we model that?
00:02:18 Samir: we usually recommend a queueing model approach: treat requests as M/M/c with a prioritized queue for low-latency traffic. Baseline capacity sized to satisfy the desired P95 under expected steady rps; burst handles short spikes, with a limited queue depth for best-effort traffic. We can provide a spreadsheet model.
00:02:39 Priya: can that queueing be surfaced per-route? we have critical routes for user-facing features and cheaper async routes for batch.
00:02:47 Nora: yes, per-route SLA & routing policies are first-class. you can pin routes to dedicated GPU classes, set queue priority, or route to a lower-cost quantized variant for async.
00:02:58 Jordan: you mentioned quantized variants — how much perf/cost delta are we talking for 13B quantized vs fp16?
00:03:06 Samir: for 13B: 4-bit quantized usually yields ~2.5-3x token throughput improvement and 2-3x cost reduction, but depending on your quality tolerance there may be small output drift for some tasks. 70B quantization helps similarly, but kernel availability and attention optimizations matter. We advise A/B evals on your prompt set.
00:03:28 Sam: for us, fidelity on summarization is critical — small hallucinations are bad. we need a plan for quality monitoring.
00:03:35 Alex: Redwood Optimize has quality regression alerts tied to prompt sets, we can hook your test prompts into the eval pipeline and set thresholds, then route failing traffic to a higher-fidelity variant automatically.
00:03:47 Marta (Security): on the security front: does pre-warming or cache sharing ever persist customer data across pools? we need KMS + no-shared-kv guarantees.
00:03:57 Nora: we isolate KV caches per customer; no KV sharing. For Private deployments we can use your KMS/HSM, and access controls ensure model and cache isolation. We'll share SOC2 and ISO docs.
00:04:12 Ethan: what's the behavior when burst capacity is exhausted? do you queue or degrade?
00:04:18 Samir: there's a configurable policy. default is: if reserved + burst exhausted, a short queue (configurable depth/time) holds requests; beyond that you get rate-limited errors. You can also configure automatic fallback to smaller quantized variants or region-based failover.
00:04:34 Jordan: show us latency numbers — like P50/P95 for our profile with reserved GPUs and burst.
00:04:41 Samir: sure, i'm pulling some examples. For a 13B quantized model on A100-class GPUs with batching tuned: P50 ~22ms per token, P95 ~120-180ms per token for interactive prompts of ~180 tokens, end-to-end response around 4-8s depending on sequence. With a warm baseline sized for 220 rps and batching window 5-10ms, you'd see much lower overhead.
00:05:08 Priya: batching window — can we control max latency vs throughput tradeoff? we can't add 50ms per request if we're latency sensitive.
00:05:15 Samir: yep you can set max batching window and max batch size. Redwood's continuous batching tries to keep windows tight for latency-sensitive routes and only expands for high-throughput. There's also per-route config so critical APIs get small batch windows.
00:05:29 Priya: what's the observed impact of KV cache warmup on initial request latency?
00:05:34 Samir: first request that requires KV entries will be slower; but we persist per-session KV for an active connection. Warmup strategies include: pre-warming with representative prefixes, use of cached prefixes in Redis-like store, or pushing checkpointed KV snapshots to the runtime. Warmup reduces tail by ~30-70% depending on prompt reuse.
00:05:54 Jordan: queueing model math — can you email the spreadsheet?
00:05:58 Alex: yes, we'll email the capacity planning spreadsheet with examples and a scenario tuned to your histograms.
00:06:04 Priya: about reserved GPUs: how do you recommend we split between steady baseline and burst? we have predictable daily curve with spikes up to 1.8x for 5-10 minutes several times per hour.
00:06:16 Samir: common pattern: reserve 70-80% of anticipated sustained capacity and allow burst to cover the short spikes with limits. The spreadsheet has a cost-per-token model for different split ratios. For spiky patterns, you can set burst_max_instances and a cooldown so that burst doesn't spin up constantly.
00:06:33 Ethan: we have on-prem policy constraints — ephemeral instances require approval and a long spin-up. can Redwood support manual approval gating for burst?
00:06:41 Nora: yes for Private/on-prem we can configure manual scaling hooks or sync to your change control system; Redwood's control plane can optionally only recommend burst but not auto-provision without a green light.
00:06:54 Marta: network egress and VPC peering — for private deployments we require traffic stay in our VPC and fixed IPs for allow-listing.
00:07:02 Nora: supported. we can provide NAT/static egress IPs, VPC peering, or on-prem air-gapped bundles.}
00:07:12 Alex: let me jump in with a short example scenario mapped to your numbers. if you size baseline for 180 rps at median tokens 180 on 13B quantized, you'll need roughly N GPUs (we'll send the exact calc) to keep P95 under 5s. Add burst capacity sized to handle peaks to 400 rps for 5-minute windows with autoscale cooldown 3 minutes.
00:07:34 Priya: curious about cost — what's the unit economics difference if we push more to quantized async buckets?
00:07:39 Samir: pushing non-critical tasks to quantized async reduces unit cost and lets reserved GPUs focus on low-latency. Typical split can reduce cost by 20-40% depending on traffic mix.
00:07:48 Jordan: how does Redwood handle model version rollouts in this autoscaling world — if we roll a model, will warm pools be drained/recreated causing cold starts?
00:07:57 Samir: rollouts are canaryed: we create a parallel pool for the new model, route a percentage, and warm the pool before ramp. You can set automatic fallback to previous model on regressions. That avoids mass cold starts.
00:08:12 Sam: what about model replication across regions for geo-resilience?
00:08:16 Nora: Redwood supports multi-region pools and smart routing by latency or cost. We replicate cached artifacts and can coordinate KV snapshots across regions but we recommend region-aware cache warmups to minimize cross-region transfer.
00:08:30 Marta: on compliance — can we run Private on our air-gapped infra? we need HSM, no external network.
00:08:36 Nora: yes, we have an on-prem package that runs the control plane in a customer network and supports KMS/HSM integration. we'll send the deployment checklist.
00:08:45 Jordan: okay any limitations on burst with on-prem?
00:08:49 Samir: burst on-prem depends on your capacity provisioning processes; if spin-up time is long, Redwood supports a pre-warmed standby pool pattern and predictive scaling using historical signals.
00:09:01 Priya: curious about a failure scenario: if a GPU node fails under high throughput, how does queueing behave?
00:09:07 Samir: runtime is built to evict in-flight requests gracefully where possible; we re-queue short requests and for long-running inference we checkpoint KV where possible and resume. There's also transparent failover to fallback models or other pools as policy defines.
00:09:23 Ethan: do we get tracing hooks to tie requests back to our SRE dashboards?
00:09:28 Nora: yes, Redwood Console emits traces and per-request metadata which you can route to your observability pipeline — we support OTLP, Datadog, and custom webhooks.
00:09:36 Jordan: can we see example configs for burst_policy and queueing_strategy?
00:09:41 Samir: i'll paste a short pseudo-config in the follow-up, but the knobs are: baseline_instances, burst_max_instances, burst_cooldown_seconds, queue_max_depth, queue_timeout_ms, route_priority, fallback_model.
00:09:58 Priya: about KV cache size — how do we set memory limits so we don't OOM?
00:10:03 Samir: you can set per-model KV cache size and eviction policies. Redwood's runtime monitors memory and will evict least-recently-used prefixes; we also expose metrics so you can tune cache_capacity per pool.
00:10:15 Alex: quick demo — we'll walk through a sample capacity spreadsheet and an autoscale config that matches your histogram. (screen share notes omitted)
00:12:30 Alex: (screen) here's the calc: using sample rps, token length, and batching window we compute required GPU seconds. baseline is X GPUs, burst Y GPUs. We'll send csv.
00:14:10 Priya: great. for the pilot, what telemetry do you need? we'd rather not send production PII.
00:14:16 Nora: we only need anonymized prompt/length histograms and latency markers; for quality evals we use synthetic prompts or a redacted test set. We'll provide guidance on redaction.
00:14:28 Jordan: what's the SLA expectations on Dedicated?
00:14:33 Alex: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency SLO targets per contract tier; we'll include specific numbers in the pilot doc.
00:14:40 Marta: re: encryption at rest — do you support bringing your own keys?
00:14:44 Nora: yes, BYOK via KMS is supported in Private and Dedicated. We'll share KMS integration docs.
00:14:50 Ethan: are there any known issues when mixing quantized and fp16 pools?
00:14:56 Samir: not from the routing side, but differences in output can occur. Redwood supports automatic quality gating and fallback to high-fidelity pools if quantized outputs fall below thresholds.
00:15:08 Jordan: can we automate scaling based on latency p95 instead of raw rps?
00:15:12 Samir: yes, autoscalers can use custom metrics including P95 latency, queue depth, or GPU utilization. We integrate with K8s HPA/VPA and custom metrics pipelines.
00:15:22 Priya: curious about billing when burst nodes spin up — billed per-second?
00:15:26 Alex: burst is billed on a per-minute granularity in Dedicated; we'll include exact billing granularity in pricing doc.
00:15:33 Sam: any guidance for handling nightly batch vs interactive?
00:15:36 Nora: recommended pattern is separation: dedicated pools for interactive low-latency, batch pools for throughput with larger batching windows and cheaper quantized variants. You can route jobs into batch queues and provision concurrency differently.
00:15:49 Jordan: ok let's recap and list next steps.
00:15:52 Alex: recap: 1) Redwood to send capacity planning spreadsheet and Dedicated pricing; 2) Helios to share traffic histogram and prompt set; 3) exchange SOC2/ISO & KMS integration docs; 4) schedule pilot week starting 2025-12-15.
00:16:10 Priya: timeline works. we'll aim to send the artifacts by 12/08.
00:16:15 Marta: i'll collect compliance ask list and send to Nora.
00:16:20 Samir: we'll prepare a test config for KV warmup and batching experiments and include recommended default knobs.
00:16:28 Jordan: thanks all — this was useful.
00:16:32 Alex: thanks everyone. wrapping up.

Notes/Artifacts shared: capacity_planning_spreadsheet.xlsx (link), dedicated_burst_policy_doc.pdf (link), soc2_summary.pdf (link), pilot_checklist.md (link)
